item.title: The Culture of Danger and Gender Dynamics
item.lead: The dossier contains a sharp claim about societal polarization: it states that fear of physical contact and framing normal interaction as potentially dangerous can increase the demand for digital substitutes.

blocks.text: The source describes an "offender-versus-victim matrix" in which men and women are pitted against each other. The text asserts that normal male attentiveness can be framed as suspicious in some marketing contexts, leading women to become more defensive. Simultaneously, male users could develop a fear of rejection or accusation.

This is one of the most normative and empirically ambitious parts of the dossier. The phrasing in the source is strong and sometimes establishes causality where the provided material lacks broad external substantiation. Therefore, in this PDF, it explicitly remains a source claim.

What is useful as a research question, however, is the mechanism. Can a repeated discourse of danger reduce the willingness for physical interaction? Does that change the perception of risk, trust, or dating behavior? And if so, in which populations and under what circumstances? These questions are empirically testable without validating the source claim beforehand.
Thus, the gender part of the dossier becomes less a final conclusion and more a research hypothesis about the relationship between media portrayal, social norms, and commercial substitutes.

blocks.label: RESEARCH DISCIPLINE
blocks.text: Distinguish between genuine safety problems, general societal perceptions, and the specific source claim that commercial interests systematically drive these perceptions.
